topic.angle: Modus ponens versus affirming the consequent

body.claim: From 'if P then Q' and 'Q', you cannot conclude P.
body.why: 'If P then Q' plus 'P' lets you conclude Q: that is valid reasoning (modus ponens). Flipping it is the fallacy called affirming the consequent. If an animal is a dog, it has four legs; my cat has four legs; so my cat is a dog. Many other causes can lead to the same Q.

probes.question: You know 'If P, then Q' and that P is true. What follows?
options: P and Q are the same

probes.question: True or false: 'If an animal is a dog, it has four legs. My cat has four legs. So my cat is a dog' is valid reasoning.

claims.claim: Modus ponens: from 'If P then Q' and 'P' you can conclude Q (valid)
claims.quote: Therefore, Q must also be true.
claims.note: Page: summarised as P implies Q. P is true. Therefore, Q must also be true.

claims.claim: Flipping it (from Q to P) is the fallacy of affirming the consequent
claims.quote: Both have apparently similar but invalid forms: affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent .
If an animal is a dog, then it has four legs. My cat has four legs. Therefore, my cat is a dog.

claims.claim: Many other causes can lead to the same Q
claims.quote: the consequent (a dark room) can have other antecedents (no lamp, off-lamp), and so can still be true
